## Contract

`npx hyperframes check --json` reports most violations with a `Fix:` line.

1. Every timed element has `class="clip"`, `data-start` and `data-duration` in seconds, and shows over `[start, start + duration)`: land an end state just before its end. `data-track-index` is only a Studio lane; paint order is `z-index`.
2. The video's length is the root's `data-duration`: overrun is cut, an early end holds the last frame.
3. Each composition builds one paused timeline and registers it after its tweens: `window.__timelines["<data-composition-id>"] = tl`.
4. No `Date.now()`, unseeded `Math.random()`, network fetches, timers or `repeat: -1`. Everything visible is a function of timeline time.
5. Never tween `display`, `visibility` or `autoAlpha` on a `.clip`; animate a child.
6. No CSS `transform` on an element GSAP transforms; animate transforms, not `left`/`top`/`width`/`height`.
7. Never `play()`, `pause()` or seek media. A `<video>` keeps its sound with `data-has-audio="true"`, else it is `muted`; music, voice, replacement sound and J/L cuts are a separate `<audio>`.
8. Every `<audio>` has an `id` or it is left out of the mix. No `crossorigin` on media. Time a `<video>` or its wrapper, never both.
9. Only the bundled fonts (`references/format.md`) resolve by name; any other family needs `@font-face` to a file in `assets/fonts/`.
10. Asset paths are root-relative (`assets/...`), in sub-compositions too.
11. Grades, grain, blur and vignettes on footage go through `npx hyperframes media-treatment` (`/media-use`), never CSS filters.
12. A scene file puts its styles, markup and scripts inside `<template>` and styles its root as `#root`. Intended overflow or overlap: `data-layout-allow-overflow`, `data-layout-allow-overlap`.

Studio edits the tags you write.

- One scene per sub-composition, short readable ids; the root holds only scene hosts, media and audio.
- Timed elements are written in the HTML, not made by script, each with a stable `id`.

# Animation runtimes

HyperFrames seeks each frame on its own, so motion must be a function of time, never of the previous frame. Full GSAP reference: `npx hyperframes docs gsap`.

## GSAP facts that bite

- Register the timeline last. Building inside `document.fonts.ready.then(…)` or another async callback is fine if you register at the end of it; registering first renders blank (`gsap_timeline_registered_before_async_build`).
- Place tweens at absolute seconds (`tl.to(el, {…}, 2.4)`). Set start states in the tween (`fromTo`), not in CSS.
- Measure layout once before building tweens, never inside `onUpdate`.
- Finite repeats only: `repeat: Math.max(0, Math.floor(duration / cycle) - 1)`.
- Seed randomness with a small PRNG (mulberry32).
- A scene's timeline can't reach elements outside its file, and two timelines must not animate the same property of one element.
- Transforms on a `<span>` need `display: inline-block` or `block`.
- Text that must fit a width: `window.__hyperframes.fitTextFontSize(text, { fontFamily, fontWeight, maxWidth })` returns `{ fontSize }`; `window.__hyperframes.pretext` measures text without a reflow.

## Other runtimes

| Runtime                      | Use for                           | How HyperFrames drives it                                                                        |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| CSS `@keyframes`             | Simple loops and decoration       | Found automatically; finite iterations, `animation-fill-mode: both`, `data-start` on the element |
| WAAPI                        | Native keyframes                  | `element.animate(…, { fill: "both" })` then `pause()`; times are document time, so use `delay`   |
| Lottie / dotLottie           | After Effects exports, characters | `autoplay: false`, always set `loop`, push the instance to `window.__hfLottie`                   |
| anime.js v4                  | Existing anime code               | `autoplay: false`, push to `window.__hfAnime`, `anime.createSeededRandom`                        |
| Three.js, WebGPU, p5, canvas | 3D and generative                 | Draw from `e.detail.time` in an `hf-seek` listener; set `data-duration` on the root              |

Charts and map overlays: drive them from a GSAP tween's `onUpdate`, not the library's own transitions. A real place is shown on baked imagery, not drawn (`film.md` "Maps and real places"). Heavy setup (big meshes, shader compiles) registers a `window.__hf.buildReady["<key>"]` promise.

## The seek protocol

```html
<script>
  function renderAt(t) {
    /* draw the frame for t seconds from state derived from t alone */
  }
  window.addEventListener("hf-seek", (e) => {
    renderAt(e.detail.time);
    // async work (GPU submit, image decode): e.detail.waitUntil(promise), called synchronously
  });
  renderAt(0);
</script>
```

No `requestAnimationFrame` loop or timer as the clock.

Rendering

Render compositions to MP4 with npx hyperframes render.

Local Mode (default)

Uses Puppeteer (bundled Chromium) + system FFmpeg. Fast for iteration.
Requires: FFmpeg installed (brew install ffmpeg or apt install ffmpeg).

Docker Mode (--docker)

Deterministic output with exact Chrome version and fonts. For production.
Requires: Docker installed and running.

Options

  • -f, --fps — 24, 30, or 60 (default: 30)
  • -q, --quality — draft, standard, high (default: standard)
  • -w, --workers — Parallel workers 1-8 (default: auto)
  • --crf — Override encoder CRF (mutually exclusive with --video-bitrate)
  • --video-bitrate — Target video bitrate such as 10M (mutually exclusive with --crf)
  • --vp9-cpu-used — WebM VP9 speed/quality tradeoff (-8 to 8, default: 4). Higher values encode faster with larger output / quality tradeoff.
  • --video-frame-format — Source video frame extraction format: auto, jpg, or png (default: auto). Use png for UI recordings, screen captures, and color-sensitive source videos.
  • --gpu — Use GPU encoding (NVENC, VideoToolbox, AMF, VAAPI, QSV)
  • --browser-gpu / --no-browser-gpu — Force host GPU or software (SwiftShader) for Chrome/WebGL capture. Default for local renders is auto — probe WebGL availability on first launch and fall back to software if no GPU is reachable. Docker mode always uses software.
  • -o, --output — Custom output path

Tips

  • Use draft quality for fast previews during development
  • Local renders auto-detect GPU on first launch; use --browser-gpu to force hardware (errors if no GPU) or --no-browser-gpu to force SwiftShader
  • Use --gpu when a local render also benefits from hardware FFmpeg encoding
  • Use --video-frame-format png when source videos contain saturated UI colors that should avoid JPEG extraction
  • Use npx hyperframes benchmark to find optimal settings
  • 4 workers is usually the sweet spot for most compositions

# 3D, simulations and generative pieces

Use 3D when the film earns it: an object or a set as the payoff, a product, a simulation that explains. Loading Three.js, WebGPU, p5 or canvas and the seek protocol are in `../runtimes.md`.

## Deterministic by construction

- Draw every frame from timeline time in the `hf-seek` listener; frames render out of order.
- Simulate once at load (physics, agents, particles) into arrays, then look up the state at `t`: `render(t)` stays a pure function. Heavy setup (meshes, shader compiles, the simulation) registers a `window.__hf.buildReady` promise.
- Seed every random choice; a seeded hash of the index, never `Math.random()`.

## Camera and story

- One hero object beats a crowd. Fly through or into it rather than orbiting it: one dive is worth ten turns.
- Cutaways, exploded views and chapters with one caption line each, plus labels with real numbers, turn a simulation into an explanation instead of eye candy.
- Product UI is never tilted into 3D; only generated content tilts.

## Light and materials

- Light it with a warm key, a cool rim and a dark environment with two or three soft strips; turn the environment, not the object, so highlights sweep across it; a contact shadow under the object.
- Bloom eats detail: keep it to the brightest points. Glossy metal under a low light gives white streaks: roughness about 0.45 or more, environment intensity about 0.5.
- One NaN pixel turns a whole frame black through bloom: clamp values that can divide by zero.

## Check it

Snapshot the dive and the payoff (`../review.md`); a frame that takes too long to draw slows every render, so profile the heaviest moment once.
